This file was originally posted as a mystery based on time of year for this location - extremely late, and location of the bird - the canopy of a tree.  I have since learned that this species will sing from a height of 5 to 8m, in spite of the fact it is a ground-nesting species. 

Two other factors convinced me the call is correct.  The spectral signature, while missing the first note, is very similar to one seen and recorded by another member of XC, and suggests this call is plastic, and perhaps still being learned. Finally, a friend with a very well respected ear, and years of field work with birds, heard one in early June in an adjacent county, identical to this recording.

loc: South Valley, Bernalillo County, New Mexico
rmk:
Recording on Samsung Galaxy S9+ as video .mp4, extracted via Audacity to project file, exported as .mp3.
The sound file was mildly edited in Audacity: one or two extraneous pops replaced by 0.5 second of adjacent background, and the volume was slightly amplified. This individual and others were also making "chert" calls, but none of those were recorded.
Several individuals were singing in the area as they foraged high in the newly-budding cottonwoods, and eventually I managed to see one for an extended time.
The songs were roughly evenly spaced out every ~10-11 seconds, lasting about 1.5 seconds. There was not much variability in the songs from one vocalization to another.
In reviewing the sonogram, it appears to be similar to Stephenson and Whittle Type A1: a fairly level trill (of about 13 notes) followed by a slight pitch change lower (but with some up-slurs) for 3-4 notes. My impression as I recorded it was of a slight rise during during the trill, but the sonogram shows only a small inflection upwards.

Equipment: Olympus LS-10, Sennheiser ME62 microphone, and a Telinga 22 inch dish.

rmk:
Very strange song from an adult male Common Yellowthroat.  This was a marshy patch of land consisting of cattails and rushes surrounding an 'island' of partially flooded small mesquite trees and arrowweed.   It sounds similar to a type of Wilson's Warbler song but I was drawn to the bird because the Wilson's Warblers that migrate through here do not usually sing this type of song in my experience, so I wasn't sure what it was.  The bird was being very furtive, in the vein of a Common Yellowthroat or MacGillivray's Warbler.  What first got me thinking it was a Common Yellowthroat was when I heard it do a typical COYE call from the same spot as the song was coming.  Being that the song was so weird and MGWA has a similar call I thought perhaps it was just an odd MGWA practicing its song while migrating.  I was doing a survey so I had to abandon the bird but when I came back past the spot later it was still singing from the same place so I began investigating again.  I chased it around for close to an hour, making recordings and trying to get a look at it.  Finally I zeroed in on a spot where it was singing consistently and crept to within ~15ft.  There were no other birds around.  Out from the exact spot where the singing had come from hopped an adult male COYE (albeit a little scruffy looking).  I did not see the song emerge directly from his bill.  But I saw him fly to a clump of brush not 10ft from me and immediately the same song burst forth from that very spot so I am 100% certain of the singing bird's identity.  At this point I continued to observe the bird fly from brush clump to brush clump and sing the weird song and utter typical COYE calls.  In most of the recordings I took it seems to be countersinging with COYEs nearby to some extent which seems to indicate that it knows what its song it 'supposed to' song like.  At no point during my pursuit of this bird did it ever, to my knowledge or listening, switch to the typical COYE song.  

*Note: I originally uploaded this recording as having 'seen' the bird but technically at this time I had not actually seen it.  Later uploaded recordings (XC315932 and XC315933) reflect having seen the bird and making a definitive ID.  Based on the static location, similar skulky behavior and the fact that the song was consistent over the entire time period, I am confident that this bird, recorded 2.5 hours earlier, is the same bird that was later seen and appears in XC315932 and XC315933.

loc: Midway Beach, Pacific County, Washington
rmk: So, all the Yellowthroats at Midway seem to have developed their own song style that is really fun to listen to and different from what we normally hear elsewhere in the region. There were so many Yellowthroats singing (at least a dozen actively so, who knows how many more were just listening), that they seem to have each altered their typical "witchety" song to better compete with the crowd. This one was somewhere kind of close by, but still not close enough to see, and he had a fun-to-mimic song that I have assigned the words "wippety-chew" to. He has a four-note/three-rep song, instead of the usual three-note/three-rep song. Amplified, high-pass filter to get rid of heavy noise. Weather: cool (~50 or 60 degrees F), calm, overcast. Singing in beach marshland, but higher up towards the "proper" trees and houses, in thick deciduous trees less than 2-3 meters tall. Male is only assumed, as bird was not seen.

rmk: This is the final portion of a longer (about 49-second) file which also includes sounds of me walking and pishing as well as additional calls from the bird. The sound was originally recorded with video on a Kyocera USCC-E6762 cell phone and the audio file uploaded here was extracted and converted from the mp4 file. This was an unplanned recording; this bird was unusual in this place at this date and I made the recording to document its presence. The species does not normally winter here but is common in this area in summer. I initially detected the bird because of its calls which sounded reasonably typical (to me) for the species. I did see the bird and it appeared to be a young male with an incomplete but distinctly outlined face mask. The bird stayed near the ground in some weedy growth the entire time I watched it (also typical for the species). rmk: This is an audio extract (converted, amplified) from a video recording of a series of high, thin chip calls that seem to match both to the ear and to the sonogram for Cape May Warbler, though this needs confirmation.  The calls start right away (within 1 sec.), and continue throughout at about 1.5-2 sec. intervals, not to be confused with the occasional California Towhee calls, the first of which is heard right after the first chip of interest here.  These higher chips were heard from an unseen bird calling from the crown of a tall oak tree along a freshwater slough near a lake.  The calls have an especially high pitch (8-9 KHz) in a narrow band, with the cadence and modulation that appear a very good match to known recordings for this species, such as  XC319513 - Cape May Warbler - Setophaga tigrina on this site.  However, further comparison and comment is invited.  So far, despite comparison with a number of other species (various warblers, Song Sparrow, kinglets, creeper), this seems to be the best match, but other opinions will be welcomed, and this will be put up for forum discussion.  Location map is a close approximation, though hand placed.

rmk:
Two cuts from the same male, singing what is apparently an Orange-crowned Warbler song after first light. In the first cut, he is singing and calling directly overhead in a black walnut, approximately 30ft/9m above ground. In the second cut, he was singing approximately 60ft/18m above ground in a different black walnut. In fact, each time I observed this individual, he was singing in a black walnut.

Before dawn, this same individual could be heard singing the typical Cerulean song. At dawn, this bird switched to singing this aberrant song exclusively. If I had not seen him well singing directly overhead, I would never have guessed that the sounds came from a Cerulean. Also note the buzzy flight calls in the first cut, which are typical of Cerulean Warblers and unlike anything given by Orange-crowned Warblers (or other species that have similarly-structured songs like Nashville Warbler or Wilson's Warbler).

The volume of each individual song changes with the bird's position and direction as it forages in the canopy.

loc: Marble Falls, Travis County, Texas
rmk:
Hybrid Northern X Tropical Parula. Would not let me proceed without selecting one specific species so chose to enter as "Northern" Parula based on the fact that this species breeds in this location. 

Appears to be the same bird I photographed in September of 2013. Same general area as the bird I had previously observed. Male, singing on territory. 

Lacked dark necklace of Northern but with traces of darker coloration in same area. More extensive yellow, extending down the belly. Presence of incomplete, lower eye-arc (no upper eye-arc) and blotchy, well-defined orange coloration on the breast seem to suggest a hybrid Northern X Tropical Parula. 

Knocks against pure Tropical lineage are the presence of a lower eye-arc, lack of a smooth transition of yellow-orange coloration on the breast and belly (there's a well-defined blotch of orange that doesn't "fade" into the yellow), weak, black mask and darker coloration near the throat, which hints at a breast band. 

Several years ago, there was a record of TRPA from nearby Hamilton Pool. It is possible that this bird could be the offspring if that bird nested.

rmk: Windy (10-15 mph sustained) conditions resulting in leaf noise and creaking branches. This is a longer recording  with more songs than the excerpt that is XC660602. Trees were close together,  mixed conifer and deciduous, and the bird was moving around at least 8 meters up in the trees. I could not see it. There are about 28 phrases in the first section. The ending of the song is a down then upward slur, which is like the birds in the western part of the range and was quite consistent (not the up/down chip of the more eastern birds). The forest here is mostly Northern White Pines that are about 20 meters tall, with some hemlocks and a few deciduous trees (maples and birches) mixed in. rmk: This chip note is regularly heard throughout the wintering season and is the only vocalization until just prior to spring migration when they begin singing.  My observation is that with this and other species overwintering are more vocal earlier in their arrival, and that in the case of (Myrtle) Yellow-rumps they appear to be more social at that time, concentrations thinning out throughout the winter months. The recording was made with a Sound Devices 722 and a Sennheiser ME64 placed under a tree.  I 'spished' a few times to get their attention and they dutifully came in. Originally uploaded as a mystery, this is an example of the typical song of a Black-Throated Grey Warbler in the Mt Adams area of Washington state, USA. Thanks for the ID [Ian Cruickshank](https://www.xeno-canto.org/contributor/XEIROMUDEB) and [Bruce Lagerquist](https://www.xeno-canto.org/contributor/JHFICMRVUX)

Original post:
This bird was recorded just after dawn in the Gifford-Pinchot National Forest/ Mt Adams Recreational Area as part of a soundscape. I've been able to identify other species in the recording, but am having a bit of difficulty with this one. The  birds it mostly closely resembles in song to aren't the area. The locally-known breeding birds it is similar to (i.e. Yellow Warbler) have enough differences in vocalizations that I'm doubting my ID. It's an extremely common bird in this area, but  one I don't yet know personally.

Recording characteristics: amplified, some filtering out of the low-end to focus on the bird itself. No edits. First vocalization is within one second, followed by five more at 10-15 second intervals.

Vegetation: coniferous forest, mostly douglas fir

Bird unseen

Thanks for your help!

loc: Florida Canyon, Santa Rita Mountains, Pima County, Arizona
rmk:
I was birding the upper canyon above the dam in Florida Canyon.  The RCWA has been coming to the dam and spending much time there in the afternoons.  It was early so I went exploring.  About 200 meters above the dam I was crashing through the thick vegetation trying to be quiet.  A Northern Cardinal got excited and started chipping.  Then the RCWA popped up below him.  The warbler went back to casual foraging and I followed it giving it space but staying within 60 feet.  About 10 minutes after the first encounter I turned the recorder on as I could hear the light chip calls.  It then popped out in an opening of the vegetation and started do this excited call but only briefly.

The habitat is a riparian canyon a little shy on big shade trees, steep canyon slopes with arid veg which can withstand drought.  Well below elevation with Oaks and Junipers but you start to see some specimens in the canyon.  But above the mesquite trees.
